# An object that decrypts is not an object we should trust. Here the attacker
# supplies a well-formed, correctly self-signed object taken from a different
# sesam repo: right path in the footer, valid age content, but signed by a key
# the incoming branch's audit log never pinned.

sesam-repo admin base.txt mine.txt other.txt

cp $TMPDIR/base.txt s
exec sesam add s --group admin
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'add s'

# A second, unrelated sesam repo with a secret of the same name. Its signing key
# is its own, so its objects mean nothing here.
mkdir $TMPDIR/foreign
cd $TMPDIR/foreign
exec git init
exec git config user.email test@sesam.dev
exec git config user.name 'Sesam Test'
exec sesam init --user admin
cp $TMPDIR/other.txt s
exec sesam add s --group admin
cd $WORK

# ATTACKER: import the foreign object, leave the audit log alone.
exec git checkout -b evil
cp $TMPDIR/foreign/.sesam/objects/s.sesam .sesam/objects/s.sesam
exec git add .sesam/objects/s.sesam
exec git commit --no-verify -m 'evil: foreign object'

# OURS: a legitimate change to the same secret.
exec git checkout master
cp $TMPDIR/mine.txt s
exec sesam seal
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'ours: reseal s'

# Refused: the sealer is in nobody's keyring here.
! exec git merge evil
stderr 's: invalid signature'
stderr 'does not verify - refusing to merge it'

exec cat s
stdout 'MINE'

-- base.txt --
BASE
-- mine.txt --
MINE
-- other.txt --
FOREIGN
